UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                     )
San Diego Gas & Electric Company                     )      Docket No. ER26-3896-000
                                                     )


             MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                 SAN DIEGO GAS & ELECTRIC COMPANY
    TO THE PROTEST OF THE CALIFORNIA PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION


       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission or FERC), 1 San Diego Gas & Electric Company

(SDG&E) respectfully moves for leave to answer the Protest of the California Public Utilities

Commission (CPUC) filed on October 21, 2026 (Protest) in the above-captioned proceeding. The

Protest’s jurisdictional argument overreads Commission orders regarding distinct co-location

issues and ignores decades of Commission practice accepting similar SDG&E retail transmission

rate design filings under SDG&E’s Commission-approved Appendix IX to its Transmission

Owner (TO) Tariff.

       Moreover, the Protest is substantively incorrect. SDG&E’s Medium Commercial rate

filing 2 generally mirrors the Medium Commercial rate that the CPUC approved for SDG&E’s

distribution customers in Decision (D.) 25-09-006. SDG&E’s primary reason for filing is to align

with SDG&E’s CPUC-adopted Medium Commercial customer class carve-out to its existing

combined Medium/Large Commercial & Industrial customer class at FERC.




1
  18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213.
2
  SDG&E Filing, TO Tariff Appendix IX (version 14.0.0.0) (revised) filed September 30, 2026 (SDG&E
Filing, TO Tariff Appendix IX).


                                                1
           The CPUC’s rate design objection—the share of transmission costs recovered through

SDG&E’s prevailing on-peak demand charge— is not at issue in SDG&E’s filing. Instead, it is a

challenge to SDG&E’s existing Tariff, namely Appendix IX’s longstanding 90/10 split between

non-coincident and on-peak demand charges. The Commission accepted this rate design in 2009

and the Filing does not change that aspect of SDG&E’s existing tariff. It is thus outside the scope

of this proceeding.

          That 90/10 split already applies to SDG&E’s currently combined Medium & Large

Commercial/Industrial rate class under Appendix IX. In other words, even if the CPUC’s Protest

was granted, that 90/10 split would continue to apply to SDG&E’s existing combined Medium &

Large Commercial/Industrial customer class—including to the very same customers that would

be served by the new Medium Commercial Class. The only practical result would be customer

confusion from SDG&E having a Medium Commercial Class at the CPUC but not FERC, and

the loss of the benefits of collecting 25% of costs from volumetric rates instead of demand rates

for medium commercial customers.

          Existing transmission and distribution rate designs cannot be entirely aligned. SDG&E’s

FERC proposal provides incrementally “more” alignment between transmission and distribution

rates as opposed to maintaining the status quo, which would be the result if the CPUC’s Protest

were granted. The Commission should accept the Filing as submitted, effective January 1, 2027.

I.        MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          SDG&E requests waiver of Rule 213. 3 The Commission regularly permits responses

where the information provided facilitates the decision-making process, helps resolve complex




3
     18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2).


                                                 2
 issues, clarifies the issues in dispute, or leads to a more accurate and complete record. 4 As

SDG&E believes that it can adequately address the concerns raised by the CPUC, SDG&E’s

response can aid the Commission’s deliberative process.

II.      BACKGROUND

         Appendix IX of SDG&E’s TO Tariff provides the “method by which SDG&E: allocates

Base Transmission Revenue Requirements . . . to End Use Customer classes, and designs

transmission rates applicable to such End Use Customer classes assessed by SDG&E.” 5

Appendix IX has been the vehicle for SDG&E’s Commission-jurisdictional retail transmission

rate design since SDG&E filed its original TO Tariff in 1997 to establish the rates and charges

for transmission service over its facilities whose operational control it transferred to the CAISO.

Since 2003, when SDG&E moved from stated rates to a formula rate, the Commission

determines the Base Transmission Revenue Requirements (BTRR) applicable to End Use

Customers under Appendix VIII, while Appendix IX allocates that BTRR among End Use

Customer classes and designs the rates that recover it. 6

         In 2009, the Commission accepted SDG&E’s proposal “to reduce the Non-Coincident

Demand charges and implement peak-related transmission demand changes” for a subset of

                   class. 13

           On September 22, 2025, the CPUC issued D.25-09-006, which, among other things,

created a new retail Medium Commercial class and adopted distribution rate design for that

class. 14 Because the CPUC created a new retail customer class, SDG&E filed on September 30,

2026, to revise Appendices VII and IX so that customers in that class are assigned transmission

rates under SDG&E’s TO Tariff. The filing: (i) establishes BTRR and Reliability Services (RS)

charges for the affected retail classes, including the Medium Commercial class; and (ii) updates

the transmission rate determination methodologies, including the treatment of historical sales and

demand factors where historical usage for a class becomes zero. 15

           Consistent with D.25-09-006, SDG&E’s filing proposes a blended rate design for certain

Medium Commercial class schedules: 25% of class transmission revenue recovered

volumetrically and 75% through demand charges. As a secondary step, and consistent with

SDG&E’s existing Appendix IX Tariff, the demand component is then split 90% to a non-

coincident peak demand charge and 10% to an on-peak demand charge. 16

III.       ANSWER

           A.      The Commission Has Jurisdiction Over Appendix IX of SDG&E’s TO Tariff.

           The CPUC’s Protest focuses on the Commission’s recent co-location show cause orders.

Taken to its logical conclusion, the CPUC’s argument that the “Commission [has] made it clear




13
   San Diego Gas & Elec. Co., Docket No. ER21-2540-000, at 1 & n.2 (Oct. 22, 2021) (delegated letter
order) (accepting Appendix IX, version 13.0.0, effective January 1, 2022).
14
     D.25-09-006 at 40-42.
15

16

                                                  5
 that states have jurisdiction over retail cost allocation and retail rate design” 17 is inconsistent

with the reality that SDG&E’s Appendix IX has been effective for nearly thirty years. Nothing in

those orders so broadly suggests that the Commission is divesting itself of jurisdiction after

repeatedly accepting SDG&E’s Appendix IX tariff filings. Instead, those show-cause orders are

focused on the distinct issue of co-location. The CPUC itself has previously acknowledged the

Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction over transmission rate design. 18

          The CPUC quotes the PJM Co-Location Order’s statement that states have exclusive

jurisdiction “over how to allocate the costs of all Commission-jurisdictional rates (including for

energy, capacity, and transmission) among retail customers, including allocating costs among

different classes of retail customers.” 19 Yet that statement addresses “how the costs of interstate

wholesale sales and transmission of electricity assigned to a wholesale customer are allocated

among that wholesale customer’s retail customers.” 20 SDG&E’s Appendix IX end-use class

charges are not wholesale charges assigned to a load-serving entity for state sub-allocation.

Instead, they are Commission-jurisdictional rates for SDG&E’s retail customers’ transmission

service.

          The PJM Show Cause Order does not support the CPUC’s exceedingly broad

jurisdictional claim either. 21 That order recites that the FPA reserves to states authority over

retail sales, wholesale sales not in interstate commerce, and the facilities used for the generation

 and distribution of electricity. 22 It does not say, as the CPUC suggests, that the Commission

divides a transmission revenue requirement between retail and wholesale customers and that the

States then allocate the retail share among retail classes. To the contrary, paragraph 68 of that

Order describes states’ authority in the same way as in the PJM Co-Location Order: states retain

exclusive jurisdiction over “the rate designs that determine how the costs of the wholesale sale

and transmission of electricity assigned to a wholesale customer are allocated among that

wholesale customer’s retail customers.” 23 Those statements, again, were addressing a Section

206 show cause proceeding about co-located load in PJM—not the Commission’s jurisdiction

over SDG&E’s end-use customer class rates for retail transmission service under SDG&E’s

longstanding Appendix IX to its TO Tariff that the Commission has repeatedly accepted.

          Moreover, far from suggesting that the Commission was making a broad new

jurisdictional statement, the Commission instead cautioned that the boundaries between federal

and state jurisdiction “are not hermetically sealed” and that their application “will often depend

heavily on the specific facts and circumstances presented.” 24 And the Commission added that it

“has exclusive jurisdiction over the provision of transmission service” used to serve co-location

arrangements where that transmission is in interstate commerce. 25

          The CPUC’s reliance on the CAISO Show Cause Order is likewise misplaced. That

Order discusses state authority over the recovery of transmission costs in retail rates in the

context of explaining that the cost transparency measures the Commission proposes will help

state regulators “sub-allocate” Commission-jurisdictional transmission costs among retail

 customers. But it emphasizes that the Commission can address “jurisdictional transmission

rates.” 26

           That Order also refers to the states’ “authority to set rates for different classes of retail

customers.” 27 But that phrase describes the states’ ability to incorporate Commission-

jurisdictional transmission costs “into the retail rates as they see fit”—that is, how “the wholesale

costs of providing electricity, including transmission of such electricity, to those retail customers

are recovered through retail rates.” 28 Again, this concerns the sub-allocation of costs assigned to

a wholesale customer. None of these orders address, much less displaces, the end-use class

transmission rates that the Commission has long accepted in SDG&E’s TO Tariff. And even if

those orders called for coordination with the states, a directive to coordinate is based upon the

Commission’s jurisdiction over the transmission rates at issue—not transferring that jurisdiction

to the States. In sum, the Commission’s co-location orders should not be read so broadly as to

suggest the Commission is divesting itself of jurisdiction over SDG&E’s repeatedly-approved

Appendix IX to its TO Tariff.

           B.        Prior CPUC Approval Is Not a Prerequisite to Commission Action Under
                     FPA Section 205.

           Nor is the CPUC’s contention that SDG&E “must first file an application for retail rate

design at the CPUC,” after which SDG&E’s transmission tariffs “can be conformed,” 29

consistent with the FPA. The FPA contains no such requirement. FPA section 205 entitles a

transmission owner to file changes to its Commission-jurisdictional rates. 30 The CPUC cites no

filing rights on prior CPUC review of transmission rates or allowing the CPUC to tell SDG&E

what or when it can exercise its Section 205 rights at FERC.

          C.      The Filing Assigns Transmission Rates to the Medium Commercial Class
                  Consistent with CPUC D.25-09-006.

          SDG&E respects the CPUC’s authority over matters reserved to the States, including the

definition of retail customer classes. The Filing does not intrude on that authority. SDG&E made

this filing because the CPUC approved a Medium Commercial rate class for CPUC-jurisdictional

rates in D.25-09-006.

          As noted, in D.25-09-006, the CPUC divided SDG&E’s Medium and Large Commercial

and Industrial class into a Medium Commercial class and a Large Commercial and Industrial

class, 31 and adopted a cost-based Medium Commercial class for customers with demand from 20

kW up to 200 kW. 32 The CPUC approved the migration of Schedule TOU-M customers,

previously categorized as Small Commercial customers, into the new class because their 40 kW

demand threshold falls within the 20 kW to 200 kW range. 33 The CPUC further approved the

rate schedules through which the class is served: SDG&E would migrate Medium Commercial

customers to Schedules TOU-M, EV High Power (EV-HP), or Optional Lighting TOU (OL-

TOU), and create Schedule AL-TOU-M, with a volumetric distribution rate, and Schedule DG-

R-M. 34

          SDG&E’s filing seeks the establishment of transmission rates for that same class.

SDG&E’s proposed revised Appendix IX adds a “Medium Commercial” class rate, which is

generally available to commercial customers with a Maximum Monthly Demand of at least 20

kW and below 200 kW who are not on substation or transmission level service, while customers

at or above 200 kW, customers who elect a Large Commercial and Industrial rate, and/or

customers on substation or transmission level service are classified as Large Commercial and

Industrial. 35

         SDG&E implemented the Medium Commercial class in its CPUC-jurisdictional rates on

April 1, 2026. In this filing, SDG&E thus seeks the Commission’s approval “consistent with the

Medium Commercial class definition as approved by the CPUC in D.25-09-006 and as provided

in SDG&E’s CPUC tariffs.” 36 SDG&E’s filing further provides that “End Use Customer classes

shall be determined in accordance with SDG&E’s CPUC tariffs.” 37 The Medium Commercial

class in Appendix IX is thus the class the CPUC defined, with the same eligibility criteria, and it

will remain so if the CPUC later changes those criteria.

         The rate schedules in revised Appendix IX are likewise the schedules D.25-09-006

adopted for the class: Schedules EV-HP, TOU-M, and OL-TOU, 38 and Schedules AL-TOU-M

schedules, or any reassignment of customers between classes. It simply conforms Appendix IX

           Several of the features that the Protest contends were “not reviewed” by the CPUC 40

instead follow directly from the class D.25-09-006 adopted. First, the so-called “reclassification”

of EV-HP customers is not a transmission-only reclassification. Schedule EV-HP was part of

SDG&E’s legacy combined Medium & Large Commercial/Industrial class. 41 When the CPUC

divided that class, it approved the migration of Schedule EV-HP customers to the Medium

Commercial class. 42 And D.25-09-006 directed that the EV-HP waiver balance be recovered

from the Medium Commercial and Large Commercial and Industrial classes. 43

           Under SDG&E’s CPUC tariffs, Schedule EV-HP is classified in the Medium Commercial

class in whole, “with no change to treatment of the rate schedule or customers’ eligibility.” 44

Revised Appendix IX follows that classification, placing Schedule EV-HP within the Medium

Commercial class and not among the Large Commercial/Industrial schedules, 45 and moving EV-

HP customers off the volumetric Vehicle Grid Integration rate (which is classified in the Large

Commercial & Industrial customer class) and onto the volumetric-only Medium Commercial

rate. 46

           Second, the Filing’s blended design for Schedules AL-TOU-M and DG-R-M —a

volumetric rate recovering 25 percent of the allocated revenue requirement, with the remaining

75 percent recovered through demand charges 47—parallels the distribution design the CPUC

adopted, with distribution demand costs recovered through “volumetric rates, coincident demand

charges, and non-coincident demand charges.” 48 SDG&E’s testimony explains that the class’s

default CPUC schedule, AL-TOU-M, was intended to recover distribution costs through the

same 25 percent volumetric and 75 percent demand split, and that the Filing applies that split to

Schedules AL-TOU-M and DG-R-M for transmission costs. 49

          Third, the volumetric-only transmission rate applies to customers on Schedules EV-HP,

TOU-M, and OL-TOU. 50 Those schedules already pay 100 percent volumetric transmission

rates: TOU-M and OL-TOU currently pay the Small Commercial volumetric rate, and EV-HP a

volumetric rate under the legacy class. 51 The Filing changes only which class’s volumetric rate

they pay, consistent with D.25-09-006. Customers on the class’s demand-metered schedules,

AL-TOU-M and DG-R-M, pay the non-coincident and seasonally differentiated peak period

demand charges. 52

           As such, although the CPUC in its Protest states that SDG&E must first file an

application for retail rate design at the CPUC, “after which SDG&E’s transmission tariffs can be

conformed to reflect the authorized Medium Commercial Class rate design,” 53 the Medium

Commercial class and its retail rate design were already authorized in D.25-09-006. 54 SDG&E,

again, made this filing to reflect this approved new class in its transmission rates.

          D.         The Protest’s Rate Design Objection Is, in Substance, a Challenge to
                     SDG&E’s Longstanding 90/10 Demand Charge Split, Which the Filing Does
                     Not Change.

          The CPUC’s only substantive rate design objection is related to SDG&E’s applying the

existing 90/10 split between non-coincident and on-peak demand charges that has been enshrined

in SDG&E’s Appendix IX since 2009 to this new Medium Commercial class. 55

          But that 90/10 split is not a new methodology, nor is it a part of the filing. 56 Instead, as

noted, it is an existing part of SDG&E’s FERC-approved TO Tariff, Appendix IX. SDG&E has

recovered 90% of the BTRR revenues allocated to a subset of Medium and Large Commercial

customers through non-coincident demand charges and 10% through on-peak demand charges

since 2009. 57 SDG&E’s Filing simply proposes to apply the existing Tariff split to the applicable

rate schedules in the Medium Commercial class.

           For those schedules, the 75 percent demand portion “follow[s] a rate design similar to the

previously combined Schedule AL-TOU—consisting of both non-coincident peak demand and

on-peak demand charges.” 58 Revised Appendix IX applies the same mechanism—reducing the

non-coincident demand charge by 90 percent and recovering the residual 10 percent through a

seasonally differentiated peak period demand charge—to the Medium Commercial and Large

Commercial/Industrial schedules alike. 59 The application of this existing tariff provision is

consistent with how previous SDG&E Appendix IX changes have been accepted. In 2016,

SDG&E added a Vehicle Grid Integration rate to the Medium & Large Commercial/Industrial

class to implement the CPUC’s Vehicle Grid Integration Pilot Program, and it explained that the

revisions were limited to implementing that program and did not affect any other currently

effective transmission rates. 60 In 2021, the Commission accepted revisions extending the Vehicle

Grid Integration rate to commercial electric vehicle customers on Schedule EV-HP and adding a

sub-class of the Medium & Large Commercial/Industrial class for the San Diego Unified Port

District’s Cruise Ship Terminal Account. 61

          Both of those filings left the 90/10 split in place. Neither one was treated as placing that

unchanged term—or other existing approved parts of Appendix IX—at issue. This Filing does

the same.

           Although that 90/10 split is different than the 35/65 split that was applied to the Medium

Commercial Class’s distribution rates under D.25-09-006, the latter resulted from an agreement

between the settling parties in that CPUC proceeding based upon distribution-specific design

issues, while the former, as noted, is contained in SDG&E’s existing FERC tariff and not at issue

in this proceeding. In other words, even if SDG&E had not filed to create the new Medium

Commercial class, the 90/10 split would still apply to the updated rate schedules, which would

instead be grouped into the legacy combined Medium & Large Commercial/Industrial class,

including Schedules AL-TOU-M, DG-R-M, AL-TOU-L, DG-R-L, A6-TOU and AL-TOU2.

Schedules AL-TOU-M and DG-R-M are merely the Medium Commercial versions of Schedules

AL-TOU and DG-R. 62

          As such, granting the CPUC’s protest would not address the CPUC’s seeming concern.

Transmission customers that would be moved to the CPUC-created Medium Commercial class

would instead remain in the combined Medium & Large Commercial/Industrial class where they

would continue to pay transmission charges under the existing Appendix IX rate design,

including the same 90/10 split. To put another way, if the CPUC’s protest was granted, that

90/10 split would still exist in SDG&E’s tariff and would still apply to existing transmission rate

classes—including to the very customers who would be served by the Medium Commercial

class. The only difference would be that certain SDG&E customers could avail themselves of the

Medium Commercial class rate for their distribution rates but not their transmission rates,

creating an inconsistency.
